{{Short description|Scottish mathematician (1867–1960)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2017}}
{{Use British English|date=December 2017}}
[[Doctor (title)|Dr.]] '''John Dougall''' [[FRSE]] (June 1867 – 24 February 1960) was "one of Scotland's leading [[mathematician]]s".<ref name="herald">{{citation|title=Obituary: Dr John Dougall, A Leading Scottish Mathematician|newspaper=Glasgow Herald|date=25 February 1960|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2507&dat=19600225&id=9BE1AAAAIBAJ&sjid=uaULAAAAIBAJ&pg=3608,7233563}}.</ref> Two formulas are named [[Dougall's formula (disambiguation)|Dougall's formula]] after him: one for the sum of a [[generalized hypergeometric function|<sub>7</sub>''F''<sub>6</sub> hypergeometric series]], and another for the sum of a [[bilateral hypergeometric series]].

==Life==

Dougall was born in June 1867 in [[Kippen]], a small village near [[Stirling]], [[Scotland]]; his father, a watchmaker and postmaster, had nine children, among whom John was the eldest.<ref name="mactutor">{{MacTutor|id=Dougall|title=John Dougall}}</ref><ref name="rse">{{citation|title=John Dougall|first=Ian N|last=Sneddon|journal=Royal Society of Edinburgh Year Book|year=1962|pages=33–34|url=http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Obits2/Dougall_RSE_Obituary.html}}.</ref>

He was educated locally at Kippen School. He left school at age 13 to become a post office worker, but a year later entered [[University of Glasgow|Glasgow University]], from which he earned an M.A. in 1886.<ref name="mactutor"/><ref name="rse"/> (He was later given a doctorate by the same university.)<ref name="rse"/> After graduating, he taught mathematics at the [[Royal College of Science and Technology|Glasgow and West of Scotland Technical College]] before becoming an editor and translator of mathematical publications for [[Blackie and Son]], a Glasgow publisher.<ref name="mactutor"/><ref name="rse"/> He died on 24 February 1960 in Glasgow.<ref>The MacTutor biography follows Sneddon in dating his death as 25 February but the Glasgow Herald article, published on 25 February, states his death as "yesterday".</ref>

Dougall became a member of the [[Edinburgh Mathematical Society]] in 1885, and was president of the society for 1925–1926.<ref name="mactutor"/> He won the Makdougall-Brisbane Prize of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]] for 1902–1904, and was elected a Fellow of the Society in 1921.<ref name="mactutor"/> His proposers were [[George Alexander Gibson]], Sir [[Edmund Taylor Whittaker]], [[Cargill Gilston Knott]], and [[James Gordon Gray]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Biographical Index of Former Fellows of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 1783–2002|date=July 2006|publisher=The Royal Society of Edinburgh|isbn=0-902-198-84-X|url=https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp1.pdf|access-date=20 February 2016|archive-date=24 January 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130124115814/http://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp1.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

He frequently published mathematical works in the proceedings and transactions of these two societies.<ref name="mactutor"/> He was also an honorary president of the Glasgow Mathematical Association, and in 1936 he followed [[Albert Einstein]] as Gibson Lecturer at Glasgow University.<ref name="herald"/><ref name="rse"/>

At Blackie and Son, Dougall oversaw the publication of many advanced mathematics books, not only from English authors but also translations from writings in German and Italian by [[Richard Courant]], [[Konrad Knopp]], [[Tullio Levi-Civita]], [[Vito Volterra]], and others.<ref name="rse"/> Dougall's own contributions to mathematics include works on [[Bessel function]]s, [[Mathieu function]]s, [[hypergeometric series]], and the [[Schläfli double six]].<ref name="mactutor"/><ref name="rse"/> He also made contributions to the theory of [[Elasticity (physics)|elasticity]], for which he won the Makdougall-Brisbane Prize.<ref name="rse"/>

He died at home, 47 Airthrey Avenue in [[Glasgow]] on 25 February 1960.<ref>{{cite book|title=Biographical Index of Former Fellows of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 1783–2002|date=July 2006|publisher=The Royal Society of Edinburgh|isbn=0-902-198-84-X|url=https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp1.pdf|access-date=20 February 2016|archive-date=24 January 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130124115814/http://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp1.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Publications==

Dougall translated [[Max Born]]'s critical book ''Atomic Physics'', and [[Émile Borel]]'s ''Space and Time'' into English
